title: Village Ways: Capacity Building | Studio 1947
description: How Studio 1947 became a field consulting partner for Village Ways, running digital literacy workshops on Bali Island, Sunderbans.
ogDescription: How Studio 1947 grew from print design vendor into field consulting partner for Village Ways, running digital literacy workshops on Bali Island, Sunderbans.

hero.alt: Village Ways wordmark logo lockup on a plain white background

body: When social enterprises, eco-tourism organizations and impact funds look for a consultancy partner, they aren't scanning portfolios for slick tech graphics or trendy typography. They look for an agency with real empathy, hands-on field research skills, and the ability to turn people's talents into local income.

Since we started working with Village Ways (an organization known worldwide for pioneering community-owned tourism) our role has grown from design vendor into field consulting partner. This case study shows how we moved from high-quality print production to hands-on work in the field on Bali Island, Sunderbans, helping rural homestay hosts close the digital literacy gap and tell their own stories.

Village Ways works to sustain traditional rural communities by building low-impact, community-owned tourism. Ownership stays fully with village committees. That creates lasting income while protecting cultural landscapes and the local environment.
Our work together began with building visual trust through traditional creative channels:

sections.label: Print: Brochures and Calendars
body: We made premium, tactile print brochures and community-themed calendars. They turn raw rural imagery into polished editorial layouts for international travellers looking for sustainable tourism.

body: But print materials handed out in city centres don't give a community real power. To secure the local economy for the future, community members themselves needed the skills to reach modern digital marketplaces. So on April 1st, 2026, our team went to Bali Island, Sunderbans, to run a hands-on, people-first capacity-building programme.

sections.heading: Digital Literacy Workshop with Communities
sections.label: Bali Island, Sunderbans
body: We ran the workshop in the villages themselves, sitting with the people who would have to use any of this after we left. Guides, homestay hosts, women running small enterprises, a few young people who already had phones and no idea what to do with them.

The first morning was not about phones at all. It was about finding out what actually stops someone here from posting a photograph of their own work, because it is never the thing an agency assumes it is. Four things came up again and again.

cards.title: Being seen
cards.body: A real hesitation about putting yourself in front of strangers, and very little confidence that what you have to say is worth their attention.

cards.title: The camera makes people freeze
cards.body: People who talk beautifully across a table go stiff the moment a phone is pointed at them and they are asked to perform.

cards.title: Language gets in the way
cards.body: Guides and homestay owners lose business every season simply because they cannot explain in a traveller's language what they are offering.

cards.title: Nobody had been taught
cards.body: Not a lack of ability. Just that no one had ever shown them how any of these apps work, or what the feed does with what you post.

sections.heading: Our Approach: Low-Friction Digital Workflows
body: To break these barriers down, we flipped the usual social media playbook. We built three simple, low-pressure creative workflows, each suited to a different level of digital comfort.

We took away the pressure of being on camera. Participants learned to shoot clean, steady footage of their surroundings and add their own local voiceover on top. That removed the anxiety while keeping the raw, documentary feel.

Instead of worrying about heavily edited video layouts, we set a simpler rule: One Compelling Local Story + One Striking Photo = A Perfect Social Asset. This moved the focus from software skills back to their natural strength: deep oral traditions and local knowledge.

sections.subheading: The Collaborative Account Model (Shared Community Ownership)
body: To take away the ongoing pressure of running a personal profile, we set up one shared community profile. Managed together as a team, it spreads the work of creating content, builds trust within the group and keeps the community aligned over the long term.

sections.heading: The Workshop: A 4-Phase System
body: We ran the workshop in four low-pressure steps, so people could ease into creating content in the open:

cards.title: Low-Pressure Introductions
cards.body: Melt the early hesitation. Participants introduced themselves in a relaxed, warm setting, with no mention of technology or smartphones.

cards.title: Tactical Group Storytelling
cards.body: Find hidden talents. Groups picked a local fruit or a handkerchief they had stitched themselves and built a spontaneous spoken story around it.

cards.title: Reflection & Individual Mapping
cards.body: Capture personal context. Participants mapped out activities they personally enjoy, recalling single memorable moments tied to their craft.

cards.title: Boundary Auditing
cards.body: Surface hidden fears. An open floor to name and map exactly what stops them from keeping up a presence online.

body: The activity-based exercises showed a remarkable natural creative ability among the villagers of Bali, Rangabelia and Bijaynagar:

sections.label: Natural Storytellers & Photographers
body: Participants showed an immediate, natural instinct for framing, capturing context and telling strong stories around everyday village things. For example, they mapped the medicinal benefits, cooking uses and cultural role of the local banana (Kachkala).

cards.title: Module D
cards.body: UNDERSTANDING BASIC METRICS OF SOCIAL MEDIA

body: Every participant was chosen through careful skills profiling, so that peer-to-peer mentoring on site stayed focused. They included leaders like Debaprasad Baidya, Jaya Mukherjee and Animesh Mondal.

sections.heading: What This Work Shows: Building Lasting Local Skills
body: Working with Village Ways, we showed that real design innovation is measured by human impact, local agency and what lasts after we leave. By pairing professional print work with hands-on literacy workshops in the field, we helped a vulnerable community move from dependency to running its own communication.

This project is proof for future social funds, government panels and international NGOs that we don't just hand over pretty files. We build self-sustaining digital systems that preserve local heritage, grow people's skills and directly feed local income.
